# Implement block: Bakery Flap Board (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Bakery Flap Board" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A split-flap menu board in a small bakery: a walnut-grain case with a brass rim and brass screws, under the bakery's name and a slowly drifting strip of bakery photos. Sixteen charcoal flaps per line, each split across the middle with two brass hinge pins, spell the time in words on two lines and four menu lines below, the names in cream and the prices in amber. When a line changes, every flap falls through the alphabet to its new letter with the real two-half flip, the columns setting off one after another and each landing with a small bounce; now and then the time gives way to a notice such as "Second bake at half nine". Tapping a menu line flips it to the next item and grows the line into a cream card with the item's photo, name, a line about it, its price and when it came out of the oven.

**Motion.** Each flap moves only forward through its drum (space, A–Z, 0–9, . ' & -), one character every 50 ms; a falling half turns by π·(0.35p + 0.65p²) over its step, so it speeds up as it falls. The top half of the current letter folds down about the hinge with a perspective matrix (eye 3.4 flap heights away) and darkens by up to 55% as it turns edge-on, while the next letter's top behind it is shaded by 40%·sin(angle); past vertical the flap shows the next letter's bottom half, lightening as it lands, and casts up to 40% shade on the half it covers. After the last character a flap lifts 0.3 rad and drops back over 170 ms. Columns start 28 ms apart plus a fixed jitter of up to 18 ms each, so a line ripples left to right; a change that arrives mid-flip starts from the characters showing. Tapping a menu line flips it to its next item with a selection haptic on the same frame; 0.55 s later the card grows out of the line on a spring (stiffness 170, damping 22): its frame interpolates from the line to the card, which is centred on the screen between the safe areas (4 pt wider than the case on each side, shrinking to fit a short screen), its photo framed so the item sits in the middle of the frame (each photo has a focus point and, where the subject sits near an edge, a closer crop of up to 1.7×), its corners from 5 to 24 pt, it fades in over the first 18% of the way, and its content fades in from 45% to 85% while rising 14 pt; the board dims behind a 62% black scrim. Tapping anywhere closes the card; dragging it down follows the finger (360 pt closes it fully, rubber-banding by 0.2 past open) and a release faster than 600 pt/s down, or below 60% open, closes it with the finger's speed handed to the spring and a soft haptic. Tapping a time line swaps the time and the notice. The photo strip drifts left one set of photos per 18 s at a constant speed. Without autoPlay the time lines show the device's time in words to the nearest five minutes, checked every 15 s. autoPlay loops every 18 s at a fixed time (ten past seven): menu lines change at 0.6 and 2.0 s, the time gives way to the notice at 3.4 s, a line is "tapped" at 5.0 s and its card opens at 5.55 s and closes at 8.8 s, then the lines change back at 9.8, 11.2, 13.6, 14.4 and 15.2 s and the time returns at 12.4 s, so the loop ends on the board it started with. A touch pauses the loop for 4 s (7 s when a card opens); the loop then closes the card, sets every line back and starts over. With Reduce Motion the flaps change letter without turning (top and bottom halves swap at the middle of each step), the card fades in over 0.22 s in place, and the strip holds still.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [BakeryFlapBoardDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoardDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [BakeryFlapBoard.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoard.swift)
- [BakeryFlapBoardEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoardEngine.swift)
- [BakeryFlapBoardFlaps.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoardFlaps.swift)
- [BakeryFlapBoardParts.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoardParts.swift)
- [BakeryFlapBoardWood.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Text/BakeryFlapBoard/BakeryFlapBoardWood.metal)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
